speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the comments made by the Hon. Member seem strange to me, because as we very readily realize, the current situation, the status quo has a tremendous negative impact on our economic situation and on our agreements with the Americans concerning our products. This is another reason for negotiating with the United States with the hope of reaching an agreement under which we will no longer be the victims of the protectionist measures that are now the trend in the United States. I think the Hon. Member should agree with me that the status quo is no longer acceptable. We must strive, in the interests of Canadian industries and Canadian jobs, to reach understandings with our American neighbours so that we no longer fall victim to the kind of protectionist measures that are now hitting us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, nobody is questioning that it would be advantageous if we could come to an agreement. Why is it that when the Americans put a countervail duty on our East Coast fisheries because they say we have programs that subsidize our fishing industry, unemployment insurance or support loans at low interest for modernizing ships, nobody in Canada, not the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), not the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) nor Mr. Reisman, the very astute, tough bargainer, says to the Americans: "Just a minute. You are putting a countervail duty on our fish. You have half a dozen programs, loans at subsidized rates for improving the fishing industry, subsidies to build better vessels, you have a whole range of programs"? Why is it, Mr. Speaker, that when the Americans put a countervail duty on steel yesterday, we did not say: "You have a whole series of programs to subsidize your steel industry to make it more efficient, and yet you are saying to us that you are going to put duties on our products that we try to sell to you because we have programs to help our people"? Why do we not say to the Americans: "What are you going to do about the subsidies and the assistance that you give to your industries and workers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat to my hon. colleague that, as concerns the disagreement which we are now having with the United States, it is precisely by negotiating new procedures that we can eventually avoid the need to provide such compensation for all industries. This is what we are now saying. As for what you said earlier, we are not certain either that these negotiations will be finalized. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have both repeated many times that no agreement will be signed if it is not to the advantage of our country and of jobs for Canadians.
We therefore must repeat that we shall sign an agreement only if it benefits Canadians, but there is definitely a need as we are always facing protectionist measures which harm the employment opportunities in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to follow up on questions from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I must ask the Hon. Member if this is not an Alice in Wonderland approach. The Americans have just imposed a tariff on fish. We have always had trade with the U.S. As a matter of fact, 70 per cent of our fish goes to the United States. Historically, Atlantic Canada has traded primarily with New England, as my colleagues across the way will know. The Member says we must not maintain the status quo. The fact is that the situation is getting worse. Tariffs are being imposed on fish because the Americans say we have subsidies. The irony is that the last Budget did away with those subsidies. We no longer have fishing vessel insurance. We no longer have fishing vessel subsidies. The Government has made the fishery completely user-pay. It is now charging for environmental forecasts and is charging berthing fees. Everything in the fishery is now user-pay.
The point I am making is that at a time when the Government is moving to user-pay in the fishery and eliminating subsidies, the Americans are slapping tariffs on Canadian fish, which they did not do before. What does the Hon. Member suggest we say to Canadian fishermen? Should we tell them to have faith in the Americans? Should we tell them to have faith in the negotiating process, that the status quo is not good enough and that we are going to get a better deal for them? The fact is that they see their situation worsening and going downhill. What would my colleague say to those fishermen if she were in my shoes and representing them?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion presented by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, which reads as follows:
That this House condemns the failure of the government to act in Canada's interests in the free trade discussion with the United States and, in particular, for its failure to obtain an agreement to suspend unilateral tariff action by either country during the period of these discussions.
An amendment to the main motion, on which the House will be asked to vote, was moved, adding the following:
-and for its failure to assist Canadian workers who are adversely affected by such unilateral actions.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the motion does not ask Hon. Members, at least not for the time being, to take a position for or against discussions with the United States. The purpose of the motion is to examine the way the Conservative Government has acted since the beginning of the negotiating process with the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I think we have to say that, taken word for word, the motion as amended by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), reflects a situation that is plain to see for any observer of the political scene.
Supply
First of all, before the Conservative Government came to power and hatched this plan of negotiating a free trade agreement-perhaps we should have a better definition to know exactly what we are talking about-but before the Prime Minister of Canada started these negotiations, there was no specific action by Customs to block exports of Canadian fisheries products to the United States. Before the Conservative Government started these discussions, there were no American measures against exports of agricultural products, pork in particular. Before the Conservative Government started these talks, there were no U.S. subsidies to undermine our exports or compete for international markets with agricultural products from Western Canada. Before the Conservative Government started the talks referred to in this motion, there were no tariffs to block exports of cedar shingles to the United States, and before the Conservative Government started these talks with the U.S., there was no 41 per cent tariff on certain steel products exported from Canada to the United States.
Mr. Speaker, we can only conclude that the negotiations of the Conservative Government are a dismal failure, and so it appears obvious to me that all impartial observers would readily support the motion introduced by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and amended by my colleague the Hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy).
Mr. Speaker, the incompetence of the Mulroney Government to do its job properly is there for everyone to see. This is why it should be severely censured for having so obviously failed to protect the interests of Canadians.
One might wonder why the Conservative Government, and particularly the Prime Minister, have performed so miserably. The answer is that they get off or got off on the wrong foot. Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote the remarks made by the Prime Minister no so long ago, barely a few months before the election.
Imagine, he was the Leader of the Opposition, urging Canadian men and women to support the Conservative Party. Here is what the head of the Government thought of free trade with the United States, free trade being defined as total abolition, I suppose, of tariff and non-tariff barriers, as he explained in his intervention here in the House last September when he announced the opening of free trade negotiations with the United States.
Here is what Mr. Mulroney, the present Prime Minister, the Prime Minister of Canada said a few months before becoming Prime Minister with respect to free trade with the United States. He spoke in English, so I quote him in English:

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said free trade would be "like sleeping with an elephant. If it ever rolls over, you're a dead man. And I'll tell you when it's going to roll over. It's going to roll over in times of economic depression".

June 3, 1986
Supply

This is what the present Prime Minister of Canada had to say on the concept of free trade with the United States hardly a few months before he was elected to the position he is in now. The question that comes to one's mind, without passing judgment on the substance of the free trade issue, is this: Did the Prime Minister have a mandate from the Canadian people to negotiate or to enter into such negotiations?
I suppose that historians who follow the present actions of the Government and draw a parallel with the suggestions the Tories made a few months before the election could easily recite to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) many of the speeches made by Mr. Disraeli in the British House of Commons when he was attacking his Leader, the Conservative Prime Minister Mr. Peel, on the issue of the implementation or repeal of the Corn Laws. Because at that time Conservatives in England had stated their position publicly against the repeal of the Corn Laws. Everybody recalls that. Disraeli had this to say about his Prime Minister and his Party:
A Conservative Government is an organized hypocrisy. That is what Disraeli was saying about Peel when he abolished the corn laws, because the Conservative Party of England in those years campaigned against the abolition of the corn laws. Today the Prime Minister of Canada, who campaigned against free trade, is now in full negotiations with his friend, the President of the U.S. I wonder if we can apply to this situation the same kind of speeches that Disraeli was applying to Peel about the corn laws.

There is also another aspect which tells us that this Government deserves to be condemned, as indicated in today's motion, because they launched those negotiations on a basis that is not very sound in my view. The premise to the Prime Minister's argument was the following: Let us be nice with the President of the United States, and the Americans will be nice to us. Or: Let us be nice with the Americans on a number of questions, that is money in the bank for free trade negotiations. Everybody recalls that.
He told us, when an American ice-breaker entered our waters without being invited, that it was a significant encroachment upon Canadian sovereignty. But there was the usual argument: It was money in the bank for free trade negotiations.
When the American Government and the President applied pressure to have us change the rules on screening foreign investments ... The indirect suggestion was that we should be nice to the Americans, and this will be money in the bank for the free trade negotiations.
When we amended the National Energy Program, certainly to please some very conservative circles that existed in Canada, big corporations we did that for them, but also we did that to
please the Americans because, to use the Prime Minister's terms, that was money in the bank.
I can tell you that when we consider the results, the money in the bank has not yielded much interest. Because we suddenly realize that we have a Prime Minister who has banked on his personal relations with the American President, who has said yes to the National Energy Policy and to the passage of the American icebreaker in Canadian waters, and who has accepted the NORAD agreements without saying a word. All of this because this was part of his policy to be nice to the Americans.
It is easy to see that at the international level, negotiations cannot be conducted this way. That is why the motion as amended properly reflects the reality without taking a stand for or against free trade negotiations; but it can be very easily demonstrated that this was a deplorable failure. Because there are today in British Columbia 4,000 jobs being jeopardized and in danger of being lost because the American Governe-ment has imposed a countervailing duty of 35 per cent. How many hundreds of jobs are being jeopardized by the imposition of a 41 per cent tariff on some steel products? How many Atlantic coast fishermen are affected by a specific tariff? How many hog producers? What about the agricultural policy of the United States? And they say on the Government side that the purpose of the negotiations was to stop American protectionism. What a good deal! There has never been so many tariffs, quotas, protectionist measures since this Conservative Government came to power.
Are we to conclude that because the Prime Minister is too weak and willing to go down on bended knees, the American President take this opportunity to tighten the screw?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext: The emperor has no clothes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext:
It is easy to demonstrate that until now this Government has failed completely in its negotiations with the U.S. Canadian workers in the shake and shingle industry are losing their jobs. Our fishermen are losing their markets. This morning I heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) saying we want to protect our markets. When the President wrote his letter to Senator Packwood what did he say? He said that in any agreement with Canada the U.S. will retain the right to implement countervailing measures.

Mr. Speaker, this means that at the very moment we were involved in negotiations with the United States, the U.S. President had already decided-whatever the previous speaker or the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said this morning-the American Government and the President, in a letter to Senator Packwood, had already clearly indicated that the U.S. Government intends to reserve the right to impose countervailing measures to protect American industry.
Ironically, and this shows just how poorly the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) has handled this whole
June 3, 1986

affair, a total disaster, the sectors where free trade already existed, the sectors that were not subsidized, are now the very sectors that are most severely affected.
Mr. Speaker, there is no way the Canadian Government will convince this House that the new agreements will prevent the U.S. Government from imposing countervailing measures. The American President said the exact opposite in his letter. And I don't think the President of the United States is about to lie to the Finance Committee of the U.S. Congress. So I think the Government should realize that it better not try and sell us a bill of goods.
Mr. Speaker, now about the substance of the question. I think that everyone, at least on this side of the House, and I realize that the Members of the Tory majority, even if they do not agree and they realize their Government is a failure, 1 realize they will have to vote with the majority and defeat this motion, but the fact remains that the substance of the question-
We on the Liberal side have shown during 20 years of administration-and I could go back much further than that- that the Liberal Party of Canada has always taken an open approach concerning foreign countries. We do not have to be lectured by those who today, well certainly none of us because we were not there, but I can remember a time when the Conservatives had campaigned against free trade and managed to elect their Party leader, Mr. Borden, at the end of the debate. There was something left. I think there is a lesson there, and it is that the various Government we had since then-Liberal of Conservative, but mostly Liberal-have always defended the interests of Canadians and as a result were re-elected on a more regular basis. But since then the various Governments have always kept in mind the historic example of 1910-11. Canadian men and women as well as politicians never forgot the note President Taft had sent to some people in his administration. We must remember that because history repeats itself, and I always like to quote this remark of President Truman who once said: The only part of things one does not know is that part of history which one does not remember. We must keep history in mind. With respect to the 1911 negotiations, I wonder if today a similar note might not be found sooner or later in the files of the American President.
At the time, President Taft had said: "Basically ..." As I cannot find the quote in my notes, I shall have to paraphrase it. He said something like this: "I understand the concerns of Canadians about the Reciprocity Agreement. I can understand them because, basically, this will open up many new markets and develop very close links between the two countries, and finally, Canada will become an adjunct of the United States." The quote has just been found. Here is what President Taft said in his note to the Government which was made public by accident, thus killing any chance of success that the Reciprocity Agreement might have had. President Taft had written the following:
Supply
The amount of Canadian products we would take would produce a current of business between western Canada and the United States that would make Canada only an adjunct of the United States... I see this argument made against reciprocity in Canada and I think it is a good one.

When I look at that today, I say to myself: Yes, as the Liberal Governments have always done in the past, we have to increase our markets, but we must always remember that the main thing is to protect Canada as a nation. We have to protect the integrity of the political sovereignty of this country, and I am not saying this because I want to wrap myself in the Canadian flag, but simply because, in these trade negotiations, we have to maintain our identity and political independance and not put ourselves in a situation where we would come to depend even more than we do now on the major powers, especially the United States.
The position of successive Governments, both Liberal and Conservative, since 1910 has been to choose multilateralism over bilateralism so that the integrity of our political sovereignty would be protected, and it is best protected by agreements between a number of countries of varying economic strength sitting around the same table to sign agreements such as in the case of GATT. Some might say that we have drawn all that could usefully be drawn from the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. For my part, I do not think that it is true because until now, the GATT rounds have been used only for the purpose of reducing duties, which means that they have dealt only with tariff policies, or virtually only with tariff policies plus a number of measures which prevent the Governments from granting excessive subsidies, for instance, and which allow compensatory action to be taken.
However, I think we have reached a stage where the range of action of the GATT must be widened, and this indeed is what Canada should try to have on its agenda at least for the Montevideo discussions: extending the scope of negotiations to services and non-tariff measures that hinder trade, but on a multilateral basis.
Mr. Speaker, you are indicating that my time has expired. I would like to remind you that the motion now before us is not a motion for or against freer trade. The motion now before us asks whether this Government, ever since the negotiations opened last Fall, has acted to ensure maximum protection for Canadian interests. In view of what has transpired in the areas of fisheries, farm products, forest products and steel, not to mention this newly declared tariff war, Mr. Speaker, the conclusion is quite simple-this Government has failed in its task, and the majority of members in this House should support the motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-SUSPENSION OF UNILATERAL TARIFF ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some questions I would like to ask.

June 3, 1986
Supply
I would like to make a very brief statement as a preliminary. I first heard of free trade in the House of Commons in Ottawa when it was proposed by a gentleman who lives in Vancouver and happens to be a representative of the Official Opposition in the other place. I thought it was not a bad idea since I came from Atlantic Canada and I believed that it should be pursued. Atlantic Canada has had two periods of prosperity really, the first one during the industrial revolution in the United Kingdom when we had free access to the United Kingdom's markets for whatever product from Atlantic Canada; and the second in that period of time when we had reciprocity between Canada and the United States. We have never been prosperous when we have had to trade east and west. Nor has the West been as prosperous as it might otherwise have been when it has to trade east and west.
Canada's regions are such that they either trade across the water by the most economic source of transportation or we trade north and south to the nearest market for our products. There is a great deal of merit from an Atlantic point of view to pursue free trade as was proposed by that distinguished gentleman from the other place, and constantly discussed in Canada-U.S. relations through the Canada-U.S. parliamentary association in a constructive way.
Now I have some questions. Why does Canada find itself in the position of not being able to respond to this or virtually any other difficulty in which we now find ourselves without being committed to pay compensation to the country against whose action we reciprocate? How did that happen? Why did we negotiate ourselves into that position when we started GATT negotiations in the late 1940s? Why did we sign an agreement which left a law in place in the United States which stated unequivocally that if any production in that country was damaged it could, indeed, impose a surtax? Why did we sign that document? Why have we perpetuated that document in the continued negotiations which have taken place?
These are questions which I would like to hear Members from across the way answer. Why do we expect that we can sit in this House and wash all the dirty linen that Canada might have in trade before the television, when certainly there must be some respect for those who were trying to improve the position of Canada by trade negotiations? Why are we doing this? We cannot conduct international negotiations on the floor of the House of Commons. It never was done when the former Government was in place on an extended basis, why do they want to do it now?
There have been complaints about the surcharge on fish products going from Atlantic Canada. I ask you, why did those people who were former cabinet Ministers from Atlantic Canada not speak up? Why did they not take notice to the structures in the United States which were complaining when we set up the socialist company with unlimited access to tax dollars to export fish to the United States? Why? Why are we now criticizing today's Government for acts for which today's Canadians have to pay? Why? These are questions that the
Opposition has ignored. It has ignored them utterly in its total presentation today.
Why did we sign GATT? Why did we sign a treaty with any other nation, such as the European Economic Community, which did not allow Canada an opportunity to surcharge exports of agricultural products to Canada? Why did we do that? Why are we now complaining?
If you take a glass of reconstituted apple juice today you will find that it probably came from the European Economic Community to the detriment of our trade in Canada.
I have just one more question. Why, in dealings with GATT, did we accept the subsidized product from Europe to the point that those countries sold us their wine in Canada at less than the cost of the bottles and we had no opportunity, by virtue of negotiations of the former Liberal Government since the late 1940s, to take any punitive action against them without giving compensation to the European Economic Community? We are boxed in left, right and centre by former negotiations. Let us address these things fairly and honestly.

He said that free trade with the United States was like sleeping with an elephant. If it ever rolled over, you are a dead man. He said: "I will tell you when it is going to roll over. It is going to roll over in times of economic depression". My answer to the Hon. Member would be to ask if he would be happy to have, as a minimum, the same situation that existed in Atlantic Canada before his Government took over? There was no specific duty on fish exports from the Maritimes. There was no specific duty for hog producers.

Mr. Speaker, what could I say? When I suggested in my speech we advocated freer trade, I was not looking for an argument with the Hon. Member. It has been the action of successive Governments since 1910 to open up markets, whether in the United States, whether in the Pacific Rim countries, whether in other areas of the country ... Liberals were never against freer trade, quite the opposite. We have always looked for better access to markets.
June 3, 1986

But the Hon. Member asks why we have not provided better protection under the GATT to certain markets by repealing measures that could prevent nations from imposing special tariffs on specific products? Quite simply, I would suggest to him that when the President of the United States writes a letter to Senator Packwood saying that in any agreement with Canada he will ensure that the right of Americans to impose countervailing measures will be protected, of course 1 wish every luck to the Government in trying to reach an understanding that would prevent that kind of thing.
But what we are saying is that broader agreements must be reached. We are not against freer trade, we are against the fact that this Government badly conducted negotiations from the start, because we are now losing our markets. We are not protecting them, we are losing them as far as lumber, steel, fisheries and farm products are concerned. The inescapable conclusion is that this Government is a failure.
